content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Full-Text Search and Inverted Indexes"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction to Full-Text Search"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"Traditional database queries using standard relational operators like EQUAL or LIKE '%search_term%' perform poorly at scale. They require full table scans and fail to account for linguistic nuances like stemming, stop words, and relevance ranking. Full-Text Search (FTS) bridges this gap by enabling efficient, natural language queries across large text columns."},{"order":4,"type":"subheading","text":"The Architecture of Inverted Indexes"},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"At the core of modern FTS engines is the Inverted Index. While a forward index maps documents to the words they contain, an inverted index reverses this relationship. It maps individual terms (tokens) to the list of documents and positions where they appear."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Document 1: 'database design and indexing'"},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Document 2: 'advanced database systems'"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"The resulting inverted index maps terms to their document occurrences:"},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"database -> [Doc 1, Doc 2]"},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"design -> [Doc 1]"},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"indexing -> [Doc 1]"},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"systems -> [Doc 2]"},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Text Analysis and Tokenization Pipeline"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Before building an inverted index, text undergoes a processing pipeline known as tokenization and normalization. This typically includes character filtering, tokenization (splitting into words), lowercasing, removing stop words (like 'and', 'the'), and stemming (reducing words to their root form, such as 'running' to 'run')."},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"PostgreSQL Implementation Example"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"PostgreSQL provides built-in support for full-text search using the tsvector and tsquery data types, indexed via Generalized Inverted Indexes (GIN)."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"CREATE TABLE articles ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, body TEXT );"},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"ALTER TABLE articles ADD COLUMN body_vector tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', body)) STORED;"},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"CREATE INDEX idx_articles_gin ON articles USING GIN (body_vector);"},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Executing Full-Text Queries"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"Once the GIN index is established, you can run highly optimized search queries that leverage the inverted index structure to find matching documents instantly."},{"order":22,"type":"code","text":"SELECT id, title FROM articles WHERE body_vector @@ to_tsquery('english', 'database & design');"},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary and Best Practices"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"Inverted indexes dramatically reduce search latency for text-heavy workloads. When designing database schemas, ensure you choose the appropriate language analyzer, precompute vectors when write performance permits, and utilize GIN or LSM-tree-based indexes depending on your specific database engine."}]
